title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone Off Alaska; Big Skates in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska
summary:
Two federal actions just went into effect: the Coast Guard set a temporary safety zone in the waters west of the St. Thomas airport, and federal fisheries managers closed the retention of big skates in part of the Gulf of Alaska for the rest of 2025 because the annual catch limit has been reached.

The safety zone in St. Thomas is meant to keep boats clear of the area directly off the airport runway through December 31, improving safety for pilots, passengers, and people on the water. It also gives local responders a clearer space to work if needed. In Alaska, the skate closure is about protecting a species that’s already hit its yearly cap, supporting the long‑term health of the fishery and the broader marine ecosystem. Those steps can help sustain future fishing seasons and the communities that rely on them.

There are tradeoffs. In the Virgin Islands, boaters, tour operators, and water sports businesses that use the stretch of water west of Cyril E. King Airport may need to alter routes or schedules and follow new instructions from authorities. In the Gulf of Alaska, fishermen and processors who catch big skates—whether targeted or as bycatch—will have to release them through year‑end, which can reduce income, add operational complexity, and affect supply to buyers who depend on that species.

The Coast Guard is asking for public comments on the St. Thomas safety zone. You can share your views online by searching for the docket number on the federal comment website; submissions can be anonymous but will be posted publicly. The Alaska skate decision took effect immediately on November 21 to reflect the latest catch data and runs through December 31.
